lines.say: Your circuit is ready. Now let's run it on a real quantum chip.
Here's the catch: on a chip, not every qubit is wired to every other.
Picture a long dinner table where guests can only chat with their neighbours.
To reach the far end, guests swap seats, and each swap risks a spilled drink.
A chip is the same: wires join only neighbours, in a pattern called the coupling map.
A gate on two qubits, like C NOT, only works along a wire.
What if your circuit needs a C NOT between qubits that aren't neighbours?
Kiss kit's transpiler, which fits your circuit to the chip, adds swap gates.
A swap trades the states of two neighbours, like guests trading seats. Adding them is called routing.
Take four qubits in a row, and a C NOT from first to last.
Two swaps walk the first state next to the last. Then the C NOT runs.
But each swap costs three C NOTs, so one gate has become seven.
Every C NOT adds a small chance of error, called noise, so more gates mean a noisier answer.
Here's where the dinner table breaks down: a guest could always just shout.
A chip has no shortcut. Distant qubits can't interact until their states sit side by side.
The rewritten circuit may look different, but it computes the same thing. Only the noise grows.
So think like the chip: keep qubits that work together close, and circuits short.
Chips connect only neighbours, routing adds swaps, and every swap adds noise.
